cards.title: The Scholz–Brauer addition-chain conjecture
cards.formal: For every positive integer n, is ℓ(2ⁿ−1)≤n−1+ℓ(n), where ℓ(m) is the minimum length of an addition chain for m?
cards.why: The conjecture predicts a precise relationship between optimal multiplication plans for an exponent and for its associated all-ones binary integer. Its restricted-chain theorem shows that the unresolved issue concerns how the freedom to reuse older values affects the best possible length.

progress.text: Brauer proves the inequality for the minimum star-chain length ℓ*, as recorded in Wallner’s Section 7.
Tall, Theorems 2–4, proves the conjecture for a specified infinite family with seven binary ones and ℓ(2n)=ℓ(n), and for its doubles.
Wallner states the unrestricted Scholz–Brauer inequality among open addition-chain problems and distinguishes the star-chain result.
Agama’s preprint claims asymptotic density one and explicitly leaves the uniform all-integers version unanswered; not independently proof-audited.
Agama’s later preprint abstract claims the inequality for integers with an optimal chain in its quasi-closed class; abstract-only review.

cards.definitions: For a positive integer m, an addition chain of length r is a finite strictly increasing sequence of positive integers 1=a₀<a₁<⋯<a_r=m such that, for each i∈{1,…,r}, there exist j,k∈{0,…,i−1} with a_i=a_j+a_k. The indices j and k may coincide, and any previously produced value may be reused any number of times. The length counts the r additions, excluding the initial 1. Define ℓ(m) as the minimum such r; this minimum exists because 1,2,…,m is an allowed chain, and ℓ(1)=0. Only additions of two previously available numbers are allowed: subtraction, division, arbitrary preloaded constants and sums of three or more terms in one step are excluded. All additions have cost one, regardless of operand size; this is an operation-count question, not a bit-running-time bound. A star chain, also called a Brauer chain, additionally requires each step to have a representation a_i=a_(i−1)+a_j with j<i. Write ℓ*(m) for its minimum length. Thus ℓ(m)≤ℓ*(m); the conjecture uses the unrestricted ℓ on both sides. The integer 2ⁿ−1 has n ones in binary, and the quantifier includes n=1.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the inequality for every positive integer n, or give an integer n together with rigorous bounds on the two minimum lengths showing ℓ(2ⁿ−1)>n−1+ℓ(n). A positive proof may establish existence of the required chains without an efficient algorithm for finding a shortest chain. Equality is not required. Restricted-chain results, a finite verification range, and validity for a density-one set of integers are weaker than the universal assertion.

context_blocks.text: An addition chain is a plan for reusing intermediate powers. Once x^a and x^b have been computed, one multiplication produces x^(a+b). Starting from x, a chain for m therefore specifies a multiplication-only computation of x^m with one multiplication per chain step. This correspondence explains the interest in short chains; it does not include algorithms that use division or other algebraic operations.

For n=5, the chain 1,2,4,5 has length three and is shortest, since two additions can reach at most four. The conjectured upper bound for 2⁵−1=31 is therefore 5−1+3=7. The chain 1,2,3,6,12,24,30,31 attains that upper bound: its last two additions are 24+6 and 30+1. Exhibiting it checks this instance without claiming that every n admits an analogous optimal pattern.

The target compares the cost of building an integer n with the cost of building a much larger integer whose binary expansion is entirely ones. Its dominant term is n−1, with only ℓ(n) further additions allowed. Merely finding a chain of order n steps would leave the exact additive allowance unresolved.

Brauer’s theorem gives ℓ*(2ⁿ−1)≤n−1+ℓ*(n). In a star chain, every step must use the immediately preceding value. This proves the desired inequality whenever n has a shortest unrestricted chain that is also a star chain. In general, replacing ℓ*(n) by the potentially smaller ℓ(n) is precisely the distinction that the restricted result does not settle.

Tall’s 2024 paper proves the conjecture for an explicit infinite family of integers with seven ones in binary and ℓ(2n)=ℓ(n), and also for their doubles. An infinite family need not cover all possible exponents; its role here is a proved special case, rather than a resolution of the universal target.

A May 2026 preprint claims that the proportion of n≤N satisfying the conjecture tends to one as N tends to infinity. Its introduction expressly distinguishes this claim from a proof for all n. Even a valid density-one theorem can leave exceptions, and this preprint’s proof has not been independently verified in this review.

There is no contradiction in a chain for 2ⁿ−1 being shorter than the displayed bound: the conjecture is an upper bound. Nor must a positive solution provide a fast procedure for computing ℓ(n). These distinctions keep an existence inequality separate from exact-length formulas and shortest-chain optimization.

sentences: An addition chain starts at one and builds its target by repeatedly adding two already available values.
Its length counts additions and corresponds to the number of multiplications in the associated repeated-power computation.
The conjecture asks whether the minimum length for 2ⁿ−1 is always at most n−1 plus the minimum length for n.
The analogous theorem for star chains and known infinite families leave the unrestricted universal inequality open in the checked sources.
Resolving it would explain how efficiently optimal exponentiation plans can control the cost of all-ones binary exponents.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.

benchmark_selection.basis: Individual editorial review of saved titles, importance rationales, problem statements, source notes and working summaries. This is a review of importance and topical diversity, not a fresh verification of open status or completion of draft formulations. Importance scores are preserved.
